title: The Degenerated Differential Pair
intro: Resistors in the sources of a differential pair trade gain for a wider, more linear input range, exactly as degeneration does in a single CS stage.

blocks.text: Put $R_S$ in series with each source. When M2 just turns off, M1 carries all of $I_{SS}$ and $V_{GS2} = V_{TH}$. Writing the loop from one gate to the other through both sources:

blocks.tex: \Delta V_{in2} = V_{GS1} - V_{TH} + R_S I_{SS} = \sqrt{\frac{2 I_{SS}}{\mu_n C_{ox} W/L}} + R_S I_{SS}

blocks.text: The first term is the undegenerated limit $\Delta V_{in1}$, so the range over which both devices conduct grows by $R_S I_{SS}$ on each side. The characteristic becomes straighter and its slope falls.
The half circuit is a degenerated CS stage (ignoring $\lambda$ and body effect):
When $g_m R_S \gg 1$ the gain approaches $R_D/R_S$, a ratio of resistors, so it also becomes less sensitive to $g_m$ variation with process and temperature.

With a single tail source below two source resistors, each $R_S$ carries $I_{SS}/2$ at equilibrium and drops $R_S I_{SS}/2$. The tail behaves as if it needed that much more headroom: the input CM level and the lowest output voltage both rise by that amount, which costs $R_S I_{SS}$ of differential output swing.

Splitting the tail into two $I_{SS}/2$ sources, one per source terminal, and joining the sources through $2R_S$ removes the DC drop: at equilibrium no current flows in $2R_S$. For differential signals the midpoint of $2R_S$ is a virtual ground, so the half circuit still sees $R_S$. The price is that the two tail sources now contribute differential noise and offset, which a single shared source would not.

blocks.alt: Differential pair with resistor loads. The sources of M1 and M2 each go to their own current source of ISS over 2 to ground, and a resistor 2RS connects the two sources.
blocks.caption: Split-tail degeneration: no bias current in the degeneration resistor, so no headroom is lost.

blocks.text: Degeneration is the simplest linearisation of a pair. Other methods (offset pairs, cross-coupled pairs) appear in the nonlinearity chapter; Razavi returns to them in Chapter 14.

blocks.title: Range and gain with degeneration
blocks.text: A pair with $k = \mu_n C_{ox} W/L = 4\text{ mA/V}^2$, $I_{SS} = 1\text{ mA}$, $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$ gets $R_S = 200\text{ }\Omega$ in each source. Find the input difference that turns one side off and the small-signal gain, and compare with $R_S = 0$.
solution: Without degeneration $\Delta V_{in1} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 1/4} = 0.707\text{ V}$; with it, $\Delta V_{in2} = 0.707 + 0.2\text{ k}\Omega \cdot 1\text{ mA} = 0.907\text{ V}$.
At equilibrium $g_m = \sqrt{k I_{SS}} = 2\text{ mS}$, so $|A_v| = 5\text{ k}\Omega/(500 + 200)\,\Omega = 7.14$, against $g_m R_D = 10$ without $R_S$.
blocks.answer: Range grows from 0.71 V to 0.91 V; gain falls from 10 to 7.1.

blocks.title: Sensitivity to gm
blocks.text: In the pair above, process variation raises $g_m$ by 20 percent to 2.4 mS. By how much does the gain change with and without $R_S = 200\text{ }\Omega$?
blocks.hint: Only the $1/g_m$ part of the denominator changes.
solution: Without $R_S$ the gain is $g_m R_D$, so it rises 20 percent, from 10 to 12.
blocks.answer: 20 percent without degeneration, 13.5 percent with it.

blocks.title: Headroom cost of a shared tail
blocks.text: With $R_S = 200\text{ }\Omega$ and $I_{SS} = 1\text{ mA}$ fed from one tail source, how much higher must the input CM level be, and how much differential output swing is lost, compared with the split-tail version?
solution: Each $R_S$ carries 0.5 mA and drops 0.1 V, so the input CM level (and the lowest allowed drain voltage) rises by 0.1 V.

Each output loses 0.1 V of downward room, so the differential peak-to-peak swing falls by $R_S I_{SS} = 0.2\text{ V}$. The split tail with $2R_S = 400\text{ }\Omega$ between the sources loses nothing.
blocks.answer: 0.1 V higher CM level; 0.2 V less differential swing.
